The speckled blue grouper, Epinephelus cyanopodus, attains a maximum total length of 122 centimeters [Li = 122 centimeters], a size that positions it among the larger epinephelids inhabiting Indo-Pacific coral reef systems. Field surveys of adult specimens indicate that the ultimate wet weight corresponding to this length reaches 25905 grams [Wwi = 25905 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions for the species. The relationship between these two endpoints offers a useful index of condition for this commercially important serranid. Comparisons with related species such as Epinephelus fuscoguttatus reveal that the speckled blue grouper achieves a slightly more elongate body form, attaining comparable lengths at a somewhat lower body mass. These morphological features are consistent with its ecological role as a benthic ambush predator, where large body size facilitates the capture of fish and crustaceans. Reports from fisheries-independent surveys along the Great Barrier Reef confirm that individuals exceeding 100 centimeters are regularly encountered, though the largest specimens are increasingly rare due to fishing pressure.

The onset of sexual maturity in this protogynous hermaphrodite occurs when individuals reach a total length of 64 centimeters [Lp = 64 centimeters], a size threshold that corresponds to a calculated wet weight at puberty of roughly 3621 grams [Wwp = roughly 3621 grams]. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from specimens collected throughout the year indicates that the transition from female to male function typically follows the attainment of this size, though social factors can influence the exact timing of sex change. Juveniles and young adults inhabit shallow lagoons and seagrass beds, moving to deeper reef slopes as they mature. The length at which 50% of individuals are reproductively mature in this population aligns closely with estimates for conspecifics from New Caledonia, suggesting a degree of geographic consistency in this life-history parameter. Protection of individuals below this size threshold is therefore critical for maintaining spawning stock biomass.

Reproductive output in this species has been estimated by extrapolating fecundity relationships from the congeneric brown-marbled grouper, Epinephelus fuscoguttatus. At a water temperature of 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C], females release approximately 13700 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 13700 eggs per spawning event] during peak spawning periods, with spawning occurring roughly once every 1 to 2 days [F_R_i = roughly once every 1 to 2 days]. This batch-spawning strategy is typical for a serranid of this body size, with total seasonal fecundity often reaching into the millions of oocytes. Spawning aggregations form at predictable lunar phases, and the pelagic eggs are released into the water column where fertilisation occurs externally. The transparent, yolk-laden eggs are approximately 0.76 millimeters in diameter, which yields a calculated wet weight at birth for each newly ovulated egg of 0.00023 grams [Wwb = 0.00023 grams]. This modest egg size reflects the energetic trade-off between producing numerous pelagic propagules and provisioning each with sufficient yolk reserves for the early developmental period.

Hatching in this species occurs after a relatively brief incubation period. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C], the embryos complete development and the prolarvae emerge from the chorion just 5 days [ab = 5 days] after fertilisation. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva, measuring approximately 1.8 millimeters in standard length at eclosion, remains entirely dependent on its endogenous yolk reserves for the subsequent 48 to 72 hours. During this lecithotrophic phase, progressive yolk absorption fuels rapid morphological differentiation, including the development of the mouth gape and the onset of retinal pigmentation. The first exogenous feeding event occurs shortly after yolk-sac resorption, marking a critical trophic switch that often determines larval survival in the planktonic environment. Temperature exerts a strong influence on developmental rate, and the incubation duration of 5 days observed at 27.8 °C aligns well with predictions from thermal reaction norms established for other tropical epinephelids.

The maximum documented lifespan for the speckled blue grouper under natural conditions is 40 years [am = 40 years], a value derived from otolith increment analysis of specimens collected across its geographic range, with all age estimates contextualised at the ambient temperature regime of 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C]. This considerable longevity is characteristic of the genus Epinephelus, many members of which are slow-growing, late-maturing, and long-lived, traits that render them particularly vulnerable to overexploitation. Growth trajectories reveal that individuals approach their asymptotic length of 122 centimeters relatively slowly, with marked deceleration in annual increment after the onset of sexual maturity. The trade-off between somatic growth and reproductive investment becomes particularly evident when comparing size-at-age data from protected versus heavily fished populations. Conservation assessments have therefore emphasised the need for size-based harvest limits and seasonal spawning closures to protect the older, more fecund individuals that contribute disproportionately to recruitment. Sustained monitoring of age structure remains essential for evaluating the effectiveness of these management interventions.
